items.followUp: Name four everyday uses of organic compounds.

rubric.why: Food and fuels are important uses of organic compounds.
rubric.description: Identifies organic compounds as food or fuels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming food or fuel as a use.

rubric.why: Organic compounds are used to make a range of useful products.
rubric.description: Names a product made from organic compounds, such as medicines, clothing fibres or plastics.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least one valid product use.

modelAnswer: Organic compounds are used as food and as fuels such as petrol and natural gas.
They are also used to make medicines, clothing fibres and plastics.

items.followUp: State Bohr’s postulates about electron shells and the emission or absorption of energy.

rubric.why: This identifies the atom’s central structure and the particles around it.
rubric.description: States that an atom has a central nucleus with electrons around it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both the nucleus and electrons.

rubric.why: Bohr’s model allows electrons to occupy only particular orbits or energy levels.
rubric.description: States that electrons occupy fixed orbits or shells with definite energies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for fixed orbits, shells or definite energy levels.

rubric.why: Electrons in permitted stationary orbits do not lose energy by radiation.
rubric.description: States that an electron does not radiate energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy.

rubric.why: An electron changes energy when it moves between permitted orbits.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit or emits energy when it moves to a lower orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing either transition with its energy change.

modelAnswer: An atom has a small, positively charged nucleus at its centre, and electrons move around it.
Electrons can move only in certain fixed orbits, or shells, each having a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in one of these permitted orbits.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher-energy orbit and emits energy when it falls to a lower-energy orbit.

items.followUp: Explain how a sodium atom forms an ionic bond with a chlorine atom, and how two hydrogen atoms form a covalent bond.

rubric.why: Ionic bonding involves transfer of an electron from sodium to chlorine in this example.
rubric.description: States that sodium transfers an electron to chlorine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the electron transfer from sodium to chlorine.

rubric.why: Electron transfer produces oppositely charged sodium and chloride ions.
rubric.description: Shows that sodium and chlorine form Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving both ion charges.

rubric.why: The attraction between oppositely charged ions holds the ionic compound together.
rubric.description: Identifies electrostatic attraction between the ions as the ionic bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that oppositely charged ions attract electrostatically.

rubric.why: Sharing electron pairs is the defining feature of a covalent bond.
rubric.description: States that covalent bonds form when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying electron sharing.

rubric.why: The hydrogen example shows a shared electron pair and a stable duplet arrangement.
rubric.description: Explains that two hydrogen atoms share a pair of electrons to form H₂, giving each a duplet.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct hydrogen shared-pair example or its duplet outcome.

modelAnswer: In sodium chloride, a sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom.
Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻.
The electrostatic attraction between these oppositely charged ions forms an ionic bond.
In a covalent bond, atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
In H₂, each hydrogen atom contributes one electron to a shared pair, giving each atom a duplet.

items.followUp: According to Arrhenius, what ions do acids and bases produce in aqueous solution? Give one example of each.

rubric.why: An Arrhenius acid produces hydrogen ions in water.
rubric.description: Defines an Arrhenius acid as a substance that produces H⁺ ions in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both the H⁺ ion and the aqueous condition.

rubric.why: Hydrochloric acid is an example of an Arrhenius acid and produces H⁺ ions.
rubric.description: Gives a correct acid example and identifies its H⁺ ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example with the acid ion.

rubric.why: An Arrhenius base produces hydroxide ions in water.
rubric.description: Defines an Arrhenius base as a substance that produces OH⁻ ions in aqueous solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both the OH⁻ ion and the aqueous condition.

rubric.why: Sodium hydroxide is an example of an Arrhenius base and produces OH⁻ ions.
rubric.description: Gives a correct base example and identifies its OH⁻ ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example with the base ion.

modelAnswer: According to Arrhenius, an acid produces H⁺ ions when dissolved in water.
An Arrhenius base produces OH⁻ ions when dissolved in water.

items.followUp: Explain how atomic radius and ionization energy change from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: Atomic radius becomes smaller across a period.
rubric.description: States that atomic radius decreases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons in the same main shell more strongly.
rubric.description: Explains the decrease in radius by increasing nuclear charge while electrons are added to the same shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking increased nuclear charge and the same shell to the smaller radius.

rubric.why: Ionization energy generally rises across a period.
rubric.description: States that ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction of the trend.

rubric.why: Stronger attraction makes the outer electron harder to remove, so more energy is required; both the cause and consequence are needed for these marks.
rubric.description: Links the stronger attraction on outer electrons to the increased energy needed to remove one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the stronger nuclear attraction and 1 mark for stating that more energy is needed to remove an electron.

modelAnswer: Across a period from left to right, atomic radius decreases.
The nuclear charge increases while added electrons enter the same main shell, so the stronger attraction pulls the electron cloud closer to the nucleus.
Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
The outer electrons are held more strongly because of the increased nuclear attraction and smaller atomic radius, so more energy is needed to remove an electron.
